title: Scaling Strategies
description: Scale systems horizontally and vertically, optimize reads and writes separately, and use caching, CDNs, and queues to handle growing traffic without adding endless servers.

data.text: Scaling is how you keep a system fast and available as traffic grows. The right strategy depends on your bottleneck: is it CPU, memory, database queries, or network bandwidth? Senior engineers diagnose the bottleneck before choosing a scaling approach.
Scaling is also about cost. Adding servers is easy but expensive. Caching, query optimization, and smarter data modeling often give bigger gains for less money.
Vertical scaling means making a single server more powerful — more CPU, more RAM, faster disks. Horizontal scaling means adding more servers and distributing the load.

cards.title: Vertical Scaling
cards.description: Upgrade a single server to handle more load.
pros: Simple to implement — no code changes needed
cons: Hardware limits are real — you cannot scale infinitely

cards.title: Horizontal Scaling
cards.description: Add more servers and distribute requests across them.
pros: Cost can grow linearly with load
cons: Requires load balancers and session management
Stateful services are harder to scale

data.text: Most systems are read-heavy. A typical web app serves 10 to 100 reads for every write. You can scale reads with read replicas: copies of your database that handle SELECT queries while the primary handles INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE.

data.title: Read Scaling Techniques
items: Read replicas: distribute SELECT queries across copies
Caching: store frequent queries in Redis or Memcached
CDN: cache static assets and API responses at edge locations
Materialized views: pre-compute complex joins for reporting

data.text: Write scaling is harder because data must stay consistent. Techniques include sharding (splitting data across multiple databases), write-optimized data stores (like Cassandra), and event sourcing (append-only logs that rebuild state).

data.caption: Layered scaling architecture from CDN to database replicas
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    U[Users] --> CDN[CDN Layer]
    CDN --> LB[Load Balancer]
    LB --> APP1[App Server 1]
    LB --> APP2[App Server 2]
    LB --> APP3[App Server 3]
    APP1 --> CACHE[Redis Cache]
    APP2 --> CACHE
    APP3 --> CACHE
    CACHE -->|Cache Miss| PRIMARY[(Primary DB)]
    PRIMARY --> REPLICA1[(Read Replica 1)]
    PRIMARY --> REPLICA2[(Read Replica 2)]

data.text: Not every request needs an immediate response. Queue-based scaling decouples the user-facing request from the background work. When a user uploads a video, the API returns immediately while a worker process encodes it asynchronously.

data.title: Pro Tip
data.text: Before adding more servers, ask if the work needs to happen synchronously. Moving work to a queue is often cheaper and more reliable than scaling the API layer.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Vertical scaling is simple but limited; horizontal scaling is the path to high traffic
Scale reads with caching, CDNs, and read replicas
Scale writes with sharding, event sourcing, or write-optimized stores
Queue-based scaling decouples user experience from processing time
Always measure the bottleneck before scaling — guessing wastes money
data.takeaway: Scaling is not just about adding servers. It is about removing unnecessary work before it reaches your infrastructure.

items.question: When should I use a CDN?
items.answer: Use a CDN for any content that is cacheable and served to many users: images, CSS, JavaScript, and even API responses with low volatility. CDNs reduce latency and origin load simultaneously.

items.question: How many read replicas do I need?
items.answer: Start with one or two. Monitor replication lag and query load. Add replicas when the primary CPU or connection pool is consistently above 70% utilization.

items.question: Is sharding always the answer for write scaling?
items.answer: No. Sharding adds significant complexity — cross-shard queries, rebalancing, and operational overhead. Try queue-based scaling and write batching before reaching for sharding.

data.title: Scaling a Photo Sharing Platform
data.description: Your photo sharing app has grown from 10,000 to 1 million users. The database is at 85% CPU and response times have tripled. Propose a scaling plan that addresses both read and write bottlenecks, includes caching and CDN strategies, and estimates the cost impact.
data.expectedOutcome: A written scaling plan with prioritized changes, expected performance improvements, and a rough cost comparison for each option.
